articles.title: 'Completely baseless': ISRO rejects reports of privatisation, says reforms aimed at ...
articles.content: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on Sunday rejected reports and speculation that it was being privatised or that its role was being reduced, calling the assertions “completely baseless and incorrect”. “ISRO will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished,” the space agency said, asserting that it would continue to remain India’s principal institution for advanced space research and technology development, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration. The clarification came after nine ISRO employee associations sought clarity over reports that some of the space agency’s core functions could be shifted to the private sector, raising concerns over the policy, its implementation and its implications for the existing workforce. ISRO said the ongoing space-sector reforms were aimed at expanding India’s space ecosystem, with the private sector taking up the production and scaling of mature technologies while the agency focused on advanced research and next-generation missions. “What is changing is not the importance of ISRO, but the scale and structure of India’s space ecosystem,” it said. The agency said mature launch vehicles, routine satellites and other established systems could increasingly be produced by industry or public sector undertakings through competitive processes. This, it said, would allow ISRO to devote more scientific manpower and resources to frontier research, advanced technologies, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems and deep-space and planetary missions. Clarification regarding media reports on concerns relating to Space Sector Reforms and the role of ISRO ISRO’s Next Chapter: Leading India’s National Space Ecosystem There has been considerable reporting in parts of the media around the future role of ISRO including speculations… The employee associations had raised concerns following remarks attributed to IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka that ISRO could eventually stop manufacturing launch vehicles, with private companies or PSUs taking up production. Goenka, in posts on X on Sunday, also said the reforms were not aimed at diminishing ISRO, which would remain “the bedrock of the Indian space sector”. There has been some misleading narrative in the media around the future role of ISRO. Let me say it unequivocally: ISRO’ s role is by no means diminishing. It will remain the bedrock of Indian space sector. The reforms since 2020 are about expanding India’s overall space… “The reforms since 2020 are about expanding India's overall space ecosystem. The idea is to let industry increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites and other systems,” he said. ISRO said the reforms, initiated in 2020 and institutionalised through the Indian Space Policy 2023, were intended to create a larger and globally competitive space ecosystem, with industry, start-ups and academia participating across the space value chain. The agency said its focus would increasingly be on major national missions, including establishing the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035 and undertaking an Indian crewed mission to the Moon by 2040. articles.title: ISRO Will Remain Bedrock Of Indian Space Sector: IN- SPACe Chairman | Science & Tech
articles.content: New Delhi: Pawan Goenka, Chairman of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), said on Sunday that ISRO will remain the bedrock of Indian space sector, as some misleading reports surfaced around the future role of the Indian space agency. In a post on X, he said that there has been some misleading narrative in the media around the future role of ISRO. “Let me say it unequivocally: ISRO’ s role is by no means diminishing. It will remain the bedrock of Indian space sector. The reforms since 2020 are about expanding India’s overall space ecosystem. IN-SPACe will facilitate and authorise greater non-government participation, while NSIL will help commercialise mature capabilities,” Goenka mentioned. He further stated that the idea is to let industry increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites and other systems, while ISRO focuses on what it is uniquely placed to do: advanced R&D, scientific missions, strategic missions, new technologies, and infrastructure that is too complex for the private sector to develop on its own. “ISRO will remain at the core of India’s space programme leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions, including the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, an Indian crewed mission to the Moon by 2040, next-generation launch systems, and sustained lunar and planetary exploration,” he noted. The direction is not a smaller ISRO. It is a larger Indian space ecosystem, with ISRO pushing the technological frontier, he said. Earlier in the day, he said that India is targeting a major expansion in its space launch capabilities, with plans to increase the number of launches to 50 a year by 2030 as the country looks to build a full-fledged commercial space ecosystem. Goenka said the decision to open India’s space sector to private players five years ago was guided by two key objectives — enabling the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to venture into new frontiers and creating opportunities for private industry to scale up its capabilities. “Now comes the real test: scaling up. We have set ourselves an ambitious target of 50 launches a year by 2030,” he said. (IANS) Tags: ISRO New Delhi

articles.title: Nine ISRO employee associations seek clarity on proposed private-sector shift - Telangana Today
articles.content: NRI View Point cartoon My Space Reviews Education Today Property Lifestyle Home | News | Nine Isro Employee Associations Seek Clarity On Proposed Private Sector Shift Nine ISRO employee associations seek clarity on proposed private-sector shift Nine ISRO employee associations have sought clarification from Chairperson V Narayanan over reports of shifting manufacturing and operational functions to private entities. They questioned ISRO's future role, employee prospects and recruitment, while IN-SPACe chief Pawan Goenka stressed public-private cooperation By PTI Published Date - 6 September 2026, 05:27 PM New Delhi: Nine employee associations at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) have written to the space agency’s Chairperson V Narayanan, seeking official clarification on the proposed transfer of its manufacturing and operational functions to private entities. In a letter, dated September 4, the associations also raised questions about the agency’s future role, and the consequences for serving employees and future recruitment. “Private participation in defined commercial activities can coexist with a strong, publicly owned ISRO. What cannot be accepted without debate is a policy that reduces ISRO to a residual R&D (research and development) boutique while the realisation of the nation’s launch vehicles and the operation of its launch infrastructure pass out of public hands,” the letter said. It pointed to the August 21 comments made by Pawan Goenka, chairperson of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), which promotes, enables, authorises and supervises various space activities of non-governmental entities. Goenka, at a public event, reportedly said, “Eventually, ISRO will not make any launch vehicles and will not manufacture any launch vehicles. That will all be done by the private sector or PSU.” The employee associations claimed that these remarks have not been accompanied by any corresponding official communication from the Department of Space, explaining the approved policy, its legal and administrative basis, its phasing or its consequences for the existing workforce and future public recruitment. “Technology developed by ISRO is a national asset. Its transfer must be transparent, accountable and consistent with strategic, safety and employment considerations — not presented to employees through newspaper reports,” the letter said. It raised several other concerns. These include whether the design, development, realisation, integration, testing and launch of PSLV, LVM3, SSLV and successor vehicles will continue as ISRO functions or will cease. Also, it asked about the implications of the proposed shift for sanctioned strength, existing vacancies, recruitment calendar and induction of scientific/technical/administrative/industrial manpower in all ISRO centres. In a post on X on Sunday, Goenka wrote that ISRO and private companies would have to work together to ensure India reaches its target of 50 launches a year by 2030. “A goal of this scale cannot be achieved by one organisation alone,” he said. The IN-SPACe chairperson also highlighted that ISRO’s research would continue to push the frontiers of what is possible. He added, “Private industry must translate that momentum into manufacturing at scale: more rockets, more satellites, more launch capacity and new technologies.” Follow Us : Tags IN-SPACe ISRO launch vehicles LVM3 Related...

articles.title: India Targets 50 Space Launches A Year By 2030: IN- SPACe Chief | Science & Tech
articles.content: New Delhi: India is targeting a major expansion in its space launch capabilities, with plans to increase the number of launches to 50 a year by 2030 as the country looks to build a full-fledged commercial space ecosystem, Pawan Goenka, Chairman of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), said on Sunday. In a post on X, Goenka said the decision to open India’s space sector to private players five years ago was guided by two key objectives — enabling the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to venture into new frontiers and creating opportunities for private industry to scale up its capabilities. “Now comes the real test: scaling up. We have set ourselves an ambitious target of 50 launches a year by 2030,” he said. “A goal of this scale cannot be achieved by one organisation alone. Government and private industry have to build this future together,” Goenka added. He said the country’s space startup ecosystem has expanded significantly over the past five years. From a “barely a handful” of startups, India now has more than 450 space startups, reflecting the growing interest of private companies in launch services, satellites, space applications and other emerging areas. “Five years ago, when India opened up its space sector, we had two clear objectives: enable ISRO to conquer new frontiers and empower our private industry to scale up,” he mentioned. “Today, we are seeing both take shape. EOS-05 is a major achievement by ISRO, and this is just the beginning,” Goenka noted. The private sector has also begun moving beyond the development of prototypes, with an Indian private company successfully demonstrating the capability to launch a rocket into orbit. However, Goenka said the next major challenge for the sector would be to scale up operations and establish the infrastructure and capabilities needed to support a much higher launch frequency. “We have set ourselves an ambitious target of 50 launches a year by 2030,” he said, stressing that achieving such a target would require close cooperation between the government and private industry. (IANS) Tags: IN-SPACe Chief New Delhi Pawan Goenka

articles.title: India working to run hydrogen train at up to 110 kmph: Railway Board chief - DT Next
articles.content: NEW DELHI: The Indian Railways is working to operate the country’s first hydrogen-powered train at speeds of up to 110 kmph after completing trials at 120 kmph, Railway Board Chairman and CEO Satish Kumar said on Sunday. “The operational speed of the hydrogen train has so far been kept at 75 kmph. However, trials have been completed for a speed of 120 kmph. After that, efforts are now underway to operate it at a maximum speed of 110 kmph,” Kumar told reporters in Indore. He said consultations were underway with all stakeholders to decide the rail sections on which the new hydrogen train could be operated, with technical aspects and arrangements for fuel supply also being examined. Prime Minister Narendra Modi had on July 17 flagged off India’s first hydrogen-powered train, which operates on the 89-km Jind-Sonipat route in Haryana. Unlike conventional electric trains that draw power from overhead lines, the Hydrogen Fuel Cell Trainset generates electricity on board through a chemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen, with water vapour and heat as its only by-product. There is no combustion, smoke and tailpipe carbon emissions. Kumar said the country’s first Vande Bharat sleeper express was currently operating between Howrah and Kamakhya (Guwahati), while four more such trains had been completed and would be formally inaugurated in the coming days. The Railways is expected to receive 11 more Vande Bharat sleeper trains this year, Kumar said. As many as 200 Vande Bharat sleeper trains are being manufactured under the public-private partnership (PPP) model and each train would take around one to one-and-a-half years to be completed, he said. According to the official, the Railways was planning to operate 100 to 125 special trains for the Simhastha festival to be held in Ujjain in 2028 and was strengthening infrastructure for the large religious gathering. Kumar said steps were also being taken to address the problem of rats in trains, along with strengthening existing systems. He said artificial intelligence (AI) was being integrated with CCTV cameras to enhance security at railway stations and on trains. On the Rs 18,500-crore Indore-Manmad railway line, Kumar said land acquisition was progressing rapidly for the project, which was approved in the 2024-25 financial year. The ambitious project is expected to be completed in four to five years, he said. Kumar, along with senior officials, reviewed several railway projects in and around Indore, including construction of various rail lines, redevelopment of Indore railway station and other infrastructure works.

articles.title: India's First Quantum- AI University: Courses Starting in 2026 - Analytics Insight
articles.content: India’s first dedicated Quantum and AI University campus is being developed in Amaravati under NIELIT and MeitY. Initial programs are scheduled to begin in September 2026 from a temporary facility at Acharya Nagarjuna University in Guntur. Planned academic areas include quantum computing, AI, data science, semiconductor fabrication, chip design, VLSI, and high-performance computing. India is entering a new phase of deep-tech education, with the country’s first dedicated Quantum and AI University campus set to open in Amaravati. The campus will be established by the National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT). It will function under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Academic and advanced technology programs are scheduled to begin in September 2026. However, the permanent Amaravati campus is still being developed. Initial programs will run from a temporary facility at Acharya Nagarjuna University in Guntur. The initiative combines education, research, skilling, innovation, and entrepreneurship. It also brings quantum technology, AI, and semiconductor research under a single ecosystem. The proposed university campus will cover 8.5 acres in Amaravati. The project has an estimated investment of Rs. 730.7 crore over five years. The funding is proposed to come through a Government of India grant-in-aid from MeitY. The campus will focus on quantum technologies, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and emerging deep-tech fields. The university is designed for different stages of education . Students can pursue undergraduate, postgraduate, doctoral, diploma, and executive programs. That broad structure could make the campus relevant to students and working professionals. It also reflects the growing demand for specialized technology skills. Also Read: How We Selected the Top Quantum Computing Books Worth Reading in 2026 The course portfolio covers several fast-growing areas of technology. Quantum Computing will be one of the central academic fields. Students can also study quantum communication and security. These areas connect quantum technologies with communications and cybersecurity. Artificial intelligence and machine learning will form another major stream. Data science will also be part of the program portfolio. The university will go beyond software-focused subjects. Semiconductor fabrication and chip design are also included. Students can explore VLSI, embedded systems, and high-performance computing. Assembly, testing, marking, and packaging will also be covered. This combination gives the university a distinctly hardware-and-software approach. The permanent campus is planned around research and innovation infrastructure. A major facility will be the Quantum Research, Innovation and Incubation Block. The block is expected to cover around 1.2 lakh square feet. It will support quantum computing and communication research. Other planned facilities include quantum photonics and quantum security infrastructure . Cryogenic systems will support research involving specialized quantum technologies. The campus will also include cleanrooms and nano-fabrication facilities. Semiconductor technologies and chip design will receive dedicated infrastructure. High-performance computing, data centers, and startup incubation are also planned. This could create opportunities for collaboration between students and industry. The university is not designed only for traditional degree students. articles.title: Will ISRO become a 'residual R&D boutique'? Staff question private rocket push, future jobs
articles.content: Nine employee associations across the Indian Space Research Organisation have raised concerns over the future of the agency’s core functions, warning that a progressive transfer of launch vehicle and satellite work outside ISRO could affect jobs, recruitment, promotions and its in-house strategic capabilities. In a joint representation to ISRO Chairman and Department of Space Secretary V Narayanan, the associations have sought a time-bound written clarification on how far the government intends to move manufacturing and operational responsibilities to private companies and public sector undertakings. Advertisement The September 4 letter comes amid a wider transition in India’s space sector and shortly after ISRO’s successful GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission. Advertisement At the heart of the employees’ concerns is a statement attributed to IN-SPACe Chairman Pawan Kumar Goenka at a summit on August 21. “Eventually, ISRO will not make any launch vehicles and will not manufacture any launch vehicles. That will all be done by the private sector or PSU,” Goenka was reported to have said. The associations now want to know whether those remarks represent an approved Government of India policy or what they described as IN-SPACe’s “promotional outlook”. ISRO staff seek clarity on future of PSLV, LVM3 and SSLV The representation raises questions that go beyond manufacturing contracts. Employees have sought clarity on whether PSLV, LVM3, SSLV and their successor vehicles will continue to remain within ISRO’s mandate. They have also asked whether public sector undertakings have been excluded from any proposed PSLV and LVM3 transfer process and, if so, why. The letter refers to the transfer of SSLV technology and production rights to Hindustan Aeronautics Limited and reports of a similar approach being considered for PSLV and LVM3. It also cites reports that routine satellite manufacturing could move outside ISRO and that private entities could be brought into the operation of new launch infrastructure, including the Space Launch Complex at Kulasekarapattinam. The associations further referred to Goenka’s statement that about 120 ISRO technologies had already been transferred to the private sector. Their objection, they stressed, is not to the entry of Indian industry into the space programme. Instead, they want the Department of Space to define where private participation ends and what they fear could become an erosion of ISRO’s own capabilities. Employees flag jobs, recruitment and promotion concerns The representation places the workforce implications of the transition at the centre of the dispute. According to the associations, a sustained withdrawal from launch vehicle and satellite realisation could reduce in-house work and affect sanctioned staff strength. They fear it could also narrow promotion opportunities and further constrain regular recruitment to Group A, B, and C posts. Employees currently attached to development facilities could be left without meaningful work even as similar functions are performed by private contractors, the associations said. They have consequently sought details of the implications for sanctioned strength, vacancies, recruitment calendars, and induction over the next five to 10 years. articles.title: India's First Population Census With Digital Tools To Be Conducted In March 2027
articles.content: India's First Population Census With Digital Tools To Be Conducted In March 2027 New Delhi: The Central Government has announced that India’s c ensus w ill be conducted in 2027. The exercise will be conducted from March 1 for most part of the country as per the official notification. The entire census process will be carried out in two phases. Separate reference dates have been fixed for snow-bound areas as well as for the non-snow-bound regions of Goa, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, and Uttarakhand. Interestingly, the census 2027 will be India’s first Census conducted using digital tools. Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah launched the four digital platforms soft for conducting the census. The four digit tools are: Houselisting Block Creator (HLBC) Web Application, HLO Mobile Application, Self-Enumeration (SE) Portal and Census Management and Monitoring System (CMMS) Portal. Read Also: Supreme Court Dismisses Petition Seeking Exclusion Of Caste Enumeration In Population Census HLBC App creates Houselisting Blocks via satellite maps. HLO App (Android/iOS, 16 languages) lets registered enumerators collect data offline. Self-Enumeration Portal allows households to submit data online and get an SE ID, and CMMS Portal centrally monitors all census operations in real-time. Census is conducted under the provisions of the Census Act 1948 and Census Rules, 1990 and amendments made thereunder. Individual data collected in the Census is kept confidential and only aggregated data at various administrative levels is published. articles.title: India's first AI innovation city near Navi Mumbai airport gets fast-track development plan
articles.content: Navi Mumbai. (Representative Image via X). The Maharashtra government is preparing a time-bound plan to move ahead with the proposed Innovation City near Navi Mumbai International Airport, a project being developed in partnership with the Tata Group with a planned investment of $11 billion, news agency PTI reported. Chief Advisor to the Chief Minister for Investments and Strategy, Kaustubh Dhavse, said the government was working to create the conditions needed to take the project forward at scale. He was speaking at the Real Estate & Infrastructure Investors' Summit 2026 organised by NAREDCO Maharashtra in Mumbai. The 300-acre Innovation City is planned as a technology-focused development, with large artificial intelligence (AI) data centres forming a key part of the project. The proposed ecosystem will also include high-performance computing, semiconductor facilities and global capability centres. Dhavse said Maharashtra already has a strong position in India's digital infrastructure, with the state accounting for about 66 per cent of the country's data-centre capacity. The Innovation City is expected to build on this base by bringing technology companies and supporting infrastructure into one location. Maharashtra is separately pursuing a wider AI development programme, including six centres of excellence and AI Innovation Regions across the state. Adani Enterprises director Pranav Adani said the country's infrastructure and urbanisation growth would create opportunities for new economic corridors. Raymond Realty Chairman Gautam Singhania called for greater institutional funding, easier access to development finance, a framework for rental housing, GST rationalisation and faster urban redevelopment. NAREDCO India chairman Niranjan Hiranandani said the expansion of connectivity was opening new opportunities for Mumbai 3.0 across residential, commercial, logistics and data-centre development. articles.title: India to Host iBRICS Global Sovereign Capital Summit - GKToday
articles.content: Home India to Host iBRICS Global Sovereign Capital Summit India to Host iBRICS Global Sovereign Capital Summit September 5, 2026 Current Affairs Today - Latest Current Affairs - 2026-2027 The Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute (SWFI) announced on 4 September 2026 that it will convene the inaugural iBRICS Summit in New Delhi, India. The two-day event is formally titled “The Global Sovereign & Private Deal Room” and is scheduled for 12–13 September 2026 at The Oberoi, New Delhi, on the sidelines of the 18th official BRICS Leaders’ Summit. BRICS and Sovereign Capital BRICS is an intergovernmental grouping of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, and it has expanded its agenda to include finance, trade and payment systems. Sovereign capital refers to funds managed by state-owned investment vehicles such as sovereign wealth funds, public pension funds and other public capital pools. Summit Format and Participation The summit is an invitation-only event and is set to host more than 500 institutional investors, finance ministers and business leaders managing a combined $1 trillion in capital. A closed-door roundtable of 250 principals is scheduled for 12 September 2026 to discuss non-dollar settlement corridors and a proposed “Sovereign Capital Compact”. Investment Themes and Payment Systems The transaction-oriented sessions will focus on matching sovereign wealth funds, public pensions and family offices with projects in infrastructure, technology, critical minerals and energy transition. The summit will also address the integration of national fast-payment networks, including India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and Brazil’s Pix, with Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs). Important Facts for Exams The Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute is a global platform that tracks sovereign wealth funds and public investment institutions. Unified Payments Interface is India’s real-time retail payment system developed by the National Payments Corporation of India. Pix is Brazil’s instant payment system launched by the Central Bank of Brazil. Central Bank Digital Currencies are digital forms of sovereign money issued by central banks. Capital Deployment Framework The summit is designed as a deal-making forum for cross-border investment corridors among BRICS economies. The official communication did not disclose specific investment targets or identify the projects that may receive funding.
